title: Soviet troops storm Kabul
what: Soviet forces took key points in Kabul from 25 December, and on the 27th they stormed the palace of Afghanistan's president Hafizullah Amin, who was killed. Moscow installed Babrak Karmal in his place; some 30,000 Soviet troops were sent. Washington calls it a grave threat to peace; how the West will answer is not yet clear.
why: The opening move of the Cold War's last decade: it ends detente, brings the grain embargo and the Olympic boycott, and feeds the fear that sends gold to its 1980 peak. The Soviet Union will spend nine years and much of its strength in Afghanistan.

title: Polish shipyard workers win a free trade union
what: Strikes that began in Lublin in July spread to the Lenin shipyard in Gdansk, where an electrician, Lech Walesa, led the strike committee. On 31 August the communist government signed the Gdansk Agreement, which allows workers to form independent trade unions, a first in the Soviet bloc.
why: Solidarity is the first crack in the Eastern bloc; it is crushed in 1981 and returns to win the election of June 1989 that starts the revolutions of that year.

title: Reagan beats Carter in a landslide
what: Ronald Reagan won the US presidency on 4 November with 489 electoral votes to 49 and about 51 percent of the vote to Carter's 41, carrying 44 states. He promises tax cuts, less regulation and a harder line with Moscow. Shares jumped: the day after the vote the New York Stock Exchange traded a record 84 million shares, and the Dow climbed back above 1,000 for the first time since 1976.
why: Wall Street's verdict on the new president was a +10% month, one of the best of the decade; Reagan's tax cuts, deregulation and arms build-up frame the 1980s market, though the first two years bring recession under Volcker's high rates.

title: Martial law in Poland
what: On 13 December General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law to crush Solidarity. Phone lines were cut, a curfew imposed, the borders sealed and thousands of union members arrested overnight; on 16 December nine miners were shot dead at the Wujek mine. Western governments protest, but no one expects them to intervene.
why: Shows the limits of change in the East while Brezhnev's generation rules; Poland's crisis and its Western bank debts weigh on the 1980s until the round table of 1989.

title: The new American missiles arrive in Europe
what: The first US cruise missiles arrived at RAF Greenham Common in England on 13 November, and the first Pershing II launchers reached West Germany later in the month. NATO decided in 1979 to station the missiles unless the Soviet Union scrapped its SS-20s; after the first Pershings arrived, the Soviet Union broke off the Geneva talks on medium-range weapons. Peace protesters have camped outside Greenham Common since 1981, and in April some 70,000 people formed a human chain there.
why: The low point of the Cold War of the 1980s. The missiles that frightened Europe become the bargaining chip for the INF treaty of 1987.

title: Swiss voters keep their bank secrecy
what: On 20 May Swiss voters rejected, by 73 to 27 percent, a popular initiative 'against the abuse of bank client confidentiality and bank power' that would have loosened bank secrecy toward tax authorities at home and abroad. The big banks, Bankgesellschaft, Bankverein and Kreditanstalt, had campaigned against it.
why: Bank secrecy is a Swiss national institution in 1984; this beat sets up its long erosion: the dormant-accounts affair of the 1990s, the UBS tax case of 2009 and the automatic exchange of information.

title: Gorbachev takes over the Soviet Union
what: Mikhail Gorbachev, 54, was chosen on 11 March as general secretary of the Soviet Communist Party, a day after Konstantin Chernenko died. He follows three old and sick leaders who died within two and a half years: Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko. The West is trying to work out what the new man wants.
why: The man who ends the Cold War: perestroika and glasnost, the arms treaties, letting eastern Europe go in 1989, and finally the end of the Soviet Union in 1991.

title: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Geneva
what: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva from 19 to 21 November, the first US-Soviet summit since 1979. They agreed on no arms cuts, but their joint statement says a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and they agreed to meet again.
why: A Swiss stage for the thaw; the personal trust built here leads through Reykjavik to the INF treaty.

title: Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF treaty
what: President Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington on 8 December. It removes all American and Soviet land-based missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres, including the Pershing II and cruise missiles in western Europe and the Soviet SS-20s, with inspections on both sides.
why: The first treaty to abolish a whole class of nuclear weapons; with the crash of October behind them, markets had other worries, but for Europe the missile scare of 1983 is over.

title: Solidarity wins Poland's first free elections
what: In the elections of 4 and 18 June, the first partly free vote in the Soviet bloc, Solidarity won overwhelmingly: under a round-table agreement reached in April, 161 of the 460 seats in the Sejm and all of the new Senate were open to free election. Hungary has begun taking down its border fences. On the same day as the Polish vote, the Chinese army cleared Tiananmen Square in Beijing.
why: The first domino of 1989; Moscow does not intervene, and by August Poland has a non-communist prime minister.

title: The Berlin Wall opens
what: On the evening of 9 November an East German spokesman, Guenter Schabowski, announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border, effective immediately as he understood it; that night crowds pushed through the checkpoints in Berlin and the guards gave way. It follows a year of change in eastern Europe, with free elections in Poland in June and Hungary opening its border. On 17 November mass protests began in Czechoslovakia.
why: The defining moment of the arc. German shares were among the strongest in the game over the next two months (Siemens +21% in November, Daimler-Benz +34% in December) on hopes for a market of 17 million new customers, though the move is not tied to a cited report here.

title: Revolutions sweep the rest of eastern Europe
what: Presidents Bush and Gorbachev met off Malta on 2 and 3 December. In Prague the communists gave up power after weeks of peaceful protest, and the dissident playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on 29 December. In Romania an uprising that began in Timisoara on 16 December reached Bucharest, and the dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was executed on 25 December.
why: Within a year the Soviet empire in Europe is gone; the 1990s open with a peace dividend and new markets in the East.

title: The Deutsche Mark comes to East Germany
what: On 1 July the monetary, economic and social union of the two German states took effect, and the Deutsche Mark replaced the East German mark as the currency of the East. East Germans voted in March, in their first free election, for parties promising fast unity.
why: The generous exchange of East marks pushed up German spending and, with it, the Bundesbank's interest rates, which strained the European exchange-rate system until it broke in 1992.

title: Iraq invades Kuwait
what: Iraqi troops overran Kuwait on 2 August, and Iraq annexed it on the 28th. The UN Security Council demanded withdrawal and imposed sanctions; the United States began sending troops to Saudi Arabia on 7 August. Oil, which averaged 17 dollars a barrel in July, was at 28 dollars within days. Share prices fell: the S&P 500 lost 9 percent in the month.
why: The political shock behind the worst stock market month between the 1987 crash and 1998, and the start of the 1990-91 recession that costs George Bush re-election. The Middle East arc tells the war itself.

title: Germany is one country again
what: At midnight on 3 October the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic and Germany was reunited, eleven months after the Wall opened. The Two Plus Four treaty, signed in Moscow on 12 September by the two German states and the four wartime Allies, restores Germany's full sovereignty. On 20 September both German parliaments approved the unification treaty by large majorities.
why: Unification's cost, high German interest rates, and the European response to a bigger Germany (Maastricht and the euro) shape the next decade in Europe.

title: Hardliners try to topple Gorbachev and fail
what: On 19 August a committee of Communist hardliners, including the KGB chief, the defence minister and the vice-president, detained Mikhail Gorbachev at his holiday home and declared a state of emergency. Russia's elected president Boris Yeltsin rallied resistance in Moscow, waving the Russian flag, and the coup collapsed within days. Gorbachev is back, but Yeltsin holds the power, the Communist Party is being dismantled and one republic after another is declaring independence.
why: Three days that end the Soviet Union in all but name; markets dipped on the first day and recovered when the coup failed.

title: The Soviet Union ceases to exist
what: The leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared on 8 December that the Soviet Union no longer exists and founded a Commonwealth of Independent States, which eight more republics joined on 21 December. Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and handed the nuclear codes to Boris Yeltsin; the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin, and the Soviet Union was formally dissolved the next day.
why: The end of the Cold War that frames the first decade of the game. December's +11% on Wall Street was a Federal Reserve rate cut, not this, but the 1990s peace dividend and globalisation start here.

title: Maastricht: Europe agrees on a single currency
what: At Maastricht on 9 and 10 December the twelve European Community leaders agreed on a treaty for a European Union with common citizenship, foreign policy cooperation and an economic and monetary union with a single currency by 1999 at the latest. Countries must meet limits on inflation, deficits, debt and interest rates to join. The treaty still has to be ratified by all twelve, some by referendum.
why: The blueprint for the euro; its ratification troubles of 1992 and its convergence rules run through the decade.

title: Black Wednesday, and France's narrow yes
what: On 16 September Britain spent billions defending the pound and raised its base rate from 10 to 12 percent, then promised 15, before pulling sterling out of the European exchange-rate mechanism that evening; Italy's lira also left. On 20 September French voters approved the Maastricht treaty by only 51 percent, after Danish voters rejected it in June by 50.7 percent.
why: Europe's currency plan nearly breaks; the episode explains why the euro was built with a hard central bank and why Britain never joined.

title: Clinton wins the White House
what: Bill Clinton, the 46-year-old governor of Arkansas, won the US presidency on 3 November with 370 electoral votes and 43 percent of the vote, against 37.5 percent for President George Bush and 18.9 percent for the independent Ross Perot. The recession has ended, but unemployment remains above 7 percent.
why: Clinton's eight years, with deficit reduction and falling interest rates, coincide with the great bull market of the 1990s.

title: Swiss voters say no to the European Economic Area
what: On 6 December Swiss voters rejected membership of the European Economic Area by 50.3 to 49.7 percent, a margin of about 24,000 votes, on a turnout of 78.7 percent, and a clear majority of the cantons voted no. French-speaking cantons voted strongly yes, German-speaking rural ones strongly no. The government's application to join the European Community, sent in May, is now frozen.
why: The defining Swiss political vote of the game: it sets Switzerland on the bilateral path, makes Christoph Blocher's SVP the country's strongest force, and is a backdrop of the weak Swiss economy of the mid-1990s.

title: Austria, Sweden and Finland join the EU
what: Austria, Sweden and Finland became members of the European Union on 1 January, which now has fifteen members. Norway's voters rejected membership in November. Switzerland is now almost surrounded by the EU, and its government is negotiating sector-by-sector agreements after the EEA no.
why: Austria's entry leaves Switzerland and Liechtenstein as an island in the EU; it raises the pressure for the bilateral treaties.

title: Swiss banks settle the Holocaust claims
what: In August UBS and Credit Suisse agreed to pay 1.25 billion dollars to settle lawsuits brought in the United States on behalf of Holocaust victims and their heirs over dormant accounts and looted assets; the claims had sought 2.56 billion. The affair grew after a UBS night guard, Christoph Meili, revealed in January 1997 that old bank records were being shredded.
why: The end of a three-year crisis of Switzerland's image; it shows how American legal and political pressure can be brought to bear on Swiss banks, a pattern repeated in 2009.

title: Russia defaults and lets the rouble go
what: On 17 August the Russian government widened the rouble's trading band, restructured its short-term domestic debt and declared a moratorium on some foreign debt payments, a month after the IMF and others approved a 22.6 billion dollar rescue. The rouble lost more than half its value within weeks. President Yeltsin dismissed his prime minister, Sergei Kiriyenko, on 23 August. Western banks and hedge funds with Russian bonds face heavy losses.
why: The political collapse of Yeltsin's Russia set off the worst month for the S&P 500 between 1987 and 2008 (-15%), the near-failure of LTCM, and the fall of Credit Suisse (-30%) and UBS. It also prepares the ground for Putin.

title: The euro is born
what: On 1 January eleven EU countries, among them Germany, France and Italy, fixed their exchange rates irrevocably and adopted the euro, which now trades on currency markets and is used by banks and bond markets; notes and coins follow in 2002. The European Central Bank in Frankfurt sets one interest rate for all of them. Britain, Sweden and Denmark stay out, and so, of course, does Switzerland.
why: The euro makes Switzerland's neighbours one currency bloc; the franc becomes the haven Europeans run to whenever the euro is in doubt, in 2010-2012 above all.

title: Yeltsin resigns; Putin takes over
what: In a televised New Year's Eve address on 31 December Boris Yeltsin resigned as president of Russia and named his prime minister, Vladimir Putin, as acting president. Putin, a former KGB officer, became prime minister only in August. A presidential election must be held within three months.
why: The start of the Putin era, which leads to Georgia, Crimea and the war of 2022.

title: Swiss voters back the bilateral treaties with the EU
what: On 21 May Swiss voters approved the seven sector agreements with the European Union, Bilaterals I, by 67.2 percent. They cover the free movement of people, land and air transport, trade barriers, farm goods, research and public procurement.
why: The bilateral path is Switzerland's answer to the EEA no and the base of its relations with the EU until today; the free movement of people becomes the political fault line of the 2014 vote.

title: The Supreme Court decides the election for Bush
what: Five weeks after the vote of 7 November, the US Supreme Court stopped the Florida recount on 12 December in Bush v. Gore, and Al Gore conceded the next day. George W. Bush won Florida by 537 votes and the electoral college by 271 to 266, while Gore won more votes nationwide.
why: Bush's presidency is defined by 9/11 and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq; the long count added to the nerves of a market already falling from the dotcom peak.

title: Terror attacks on New York and Washington
what: On 11 September nineteen hijackers seized four airliners; two destroyed the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, one hit the Pentagon and one crashed in Pennsylvania. Thousands are dead. Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, is blamed. The New York Stock Exchange stayed closed until 17 September, when the Dow fell 684 points, or 7.1 percent, its largest point fall ever; airline, insurance and travel shares fell hardest. Congress voted 15 billion dollars of aid for the airlines, and NATO invoked its mutual-defence clause for the first time.
why: The defining event of the decade's politics; it deepened the recession of 2001, hit Boeing (-35% in the month) and the airlines, and leads to the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. The final death toll was 2,977 victims.

title: Swissair grounded
what: On 2 October Swissair grounded its entire fleet when fuel suppliers refused to fill its planes without cash and UBS would not release a bridging loan for daily operations; thousands of passengers were stranded around the world. Federal President Moritz Leuenberger called it a disaster and blamed UBS and Credit Suisse for abandoning the airline, and angry crowds protested at the UBS headquarters. The government granted a bridging loan of 450 million francs on 3 October so that flights could resume, and a new airline is to be built around Crossair. On 7 October the United States began bombing Afghanistan.
why: A national trauma: the flag carrier, a symbol of Swiss reliability, failed, and the big banks were blamed. It is the first of three moments (with UBS in 2008 and Credit Suisse in 2023) when the state had to step in for a Swiss icon.

title: Euro notes and coins arrive
what: On 1 January euro banknotes and coins went into circulation in twelve countries, replacing the mark, the franc, the lira and nine other currencies, which will cease to be legal tender by the end of February. The euro has been used on currency and bond markets since January 1999 and fell against the dollar until late 2000.
why: The euro becomes real for the family across the border; the currency that started weak in 1999 rises against the dollar over the following years.

title: Switzerland votes to join the United Nations
what: On 3 March Swiss voters approved joining the United Nations by 54.6 percent, with 11 full and 2 half cantons in favour, a narrow majority of the cantons. Switzerland hosts the UN's European headquarters in Geneva but has so far stayed outside the organisation.
why: Switzerland opens up, cautiously, while keeping out of the EU; neutrality is redefined, a debate that returns with the Russia sanctions in 2022.

title: The United States invades Iraq
what: American, British, Australian and Polish forces invaded Iraq on 20 March to remove Saddam Hussein, whom Washington and London accuse of hiding weapons of mass destruction. UN inspectors had found no evidence of such weapons, the Security Council did not authorise the war, and France and Germany opposed it; millions marched against it in European cities in February.
why: Splits the West and costs America's standing; the quick fall of Baghdad on 9 April lifted markets (+8% in April), but the occupation turned into a long war. The Middle East arc tells the war.

title: Ten countries join the EU
what: On 1 May the European Union grew from 15 to 25 members: Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta. Seven of them were in the Soviet bloc fifteen years ago. Switzerland must now decide whether to extend the free movement of people to the new members.
why: The reunification of Europe after 1989; cheap labour and new markets in the East for western firms, and a migration debate that reaches Britain's Brexit vote and Switzerland's 2014 initiative.

title: The Swiss join Schengen as France and the Netherlands reject the EU constitution
what: On 5 June Swiss voters approved joining the Schengen area of passport-free travel and the Dublin asylum system by 54.6 percent. Days earlier, French voters on 29 May (55 percent) and Dutch voters on 1 June (61.5 percent) rejected the proposed European constitution, throwing the EU into a crisis about its direction.
why: Switzerland moves closer to the EU by treaty just as the EU's own voters push back; the constitution returns, renamed, as the Lisbon treaty.

title: Russia goes to war with Georgia
what: After Georgian forces moved into the breakaway region of South Ossetia on 7 August, Russia sent in troops and aircraft, drove them out and advanced into Georgia proper. A ceasefire brokered by French President Nicolas Sarkozy was agreed on 12 August. On 26 August Russia recognised South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states.
why: Russia's first war against a neighbour since the Soviet end; the muted Western response is the prelude to Crimea in 2014.

title: Bern and the National Bank rescue UBS
what: On 16 October the Swiss government and the Swiss National Bank announced a rescue for UBS: the Confederation will inject 6 billion francs of capital, and the National Bank will take over 54 billion dollars of illiquid securities into a special fund. A month after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, interbank lending has frozen; a failure of UBS would threaten the savings of a million Swiss customers and the accounts of 300,000 companies.
why: The second state rescue of a Swiss icon after Swissair; it worked (the state and the SNB earned billions from it) and led to the 'too big to fail' rules that were tested again by Credit Suisse in 2023.

title: Obama is elected president
what: Barack Obama won the US presidency on 4 November with 365 electoral votes to 173 for John McCain and 52.9 percent of the vote, the first African American elected president. He takes office in January in the middle of the worst financial crisis since the 1930s and two wars.
why: Obama's first months bring the stimulus and bank stress tests; markets bottom in March 2009 and the long bull market of the 2010s follows.

title: UBS hands client names to the United States
what: On 18 February UBS agreed to pay a 780 million dollar fine and entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department over helping Americans evade taxes, and to release information on American clients suspected of tax evasion, a breach in Swiss bank secrecy. The next day the US government sued to obtain the names of all 52,000 American clients with secret UBS accounts.
why: The beginning of the end of Swiss bank secrecy for foreign clients: within months Switzerland accepts OECD standards on tax information, and the automatic exchange of information follows years later.

title: Europe bails out Greece and sets up a rescue fund
what: On 2 May the eurozone countries and the IMF agreed a 110 billion euro loan for Greece, which can no longer borrow on the markets after admitting that its deficit was far larger than reported; Greeks protested in the streets against the spending cuts attached. A week later the EU created a European Financial Stability Facility with up to 750 billion euros to stop the crisis spreading to Portugal, Spain and others. On 6 May the Dow plunged 998 points, about 9 percent, mostly within minutes, before recovering much of the loss in a 'flash crash'.
why: The euro crisis begins in earnest: the S&P 500 fell 8% in May, and the Swiss franc began its rise as Europeans fled into it.

title: America loses its AAA rating
what: After weeks of brinkmanship, Congress raised the US debt ceiling on 2 August, and on 5 August Standard and Poor's cut America's credit rating from AAA to AA+ for the first time, citing the weakened predictability of American policymaking. On 8 August all three major US indexes fell by 5 to 7 percent. In Europe, fear spread from Greece to Italy and Spain, and investors fled into the Swiss franc and gold.
why: A political rather than an economic downgrade; with the euro crisis it made August-September 2011 a bad stretch (S&P -6% and -7%, Credit Suisse -20%, Daimler -26%) and pushed the Swiss National Bank to cap the franc in September.

title: Euro summit: banks to take half off Greek debt
what: In the night of 26 to 27 October euro leaders agreed that private banks will write off 50 percent of their Greek bonds, that Europe's banks must raise more capital, and that the rescue fund's firepower is to be raised to about one trillion euros. On 31 October the Greek prime minister, George Papandreou, surprised his partners by announcing a referendum on the deal.
why: Relief that the euro would hold produced the S&P 500's best month in years (+11%), with banks and miners leading; the referendum shock at month's end showed the crisis was not over.

title: Draghi: whatever it takes
what: Speaking in London on 26 July, the president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, said that within its mandate the ECB 'is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.' Borrowing costs for Spain and Italy, which had climbed to danger levels, fell after the speech.
why: The turning point of the euro crisis: the bond-buying programme announced in September is never used, but the promise ends the panic.

title: Swiss voters back limits on immigration
what: On 9 February Swiss voters accepted the SVP's initiative 'against mass immigration' by 50.3 percent, a margin of 19,526 votes, and a majority of cantons. It requires quotas on immigration within three years, which contradicts the free movement of people agreed with the EU in the bilateral treaties. Brussels warned that free movement is not negotiable.
why: Puts the bilateral path in question for years; parliament later implements it without quotas, and the question of Switzerland's relationship with the EU stays open into the 2020s.

title: Russia annexes Crimea
what: After Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych fled Kyiv in February, soldiers without insignia seized Crimea's parliament and key sites. A referendum under occupation on 16 March was declared a vote to join Russia, and Russia annexed the peninsula on 18 March. The United States and the EU imposed sanctions and travel bans, and Russia was suspended from the G8.
why: The first annexation of territory in Europe since 1945 and the start of the war in eastern Ukraine; the sanctions are mild, and the full invasion follows in 2022.

title: Britain votes to leave the EU
what: In the referendum of 23 June, 51.9 percent of British voters chose to leave the European Union on a turnout of 72 percent. Prime Minister David Cameron announced his resignation. The pound fell to a 31-year low against the dollar and stock markets fell around the world on the day after the vote.
why: Brexit is the EU's biggest setback; the shock hit European banks hardest, Credit Suisse (-22% in June) and UBS (-17%) among them, while the S&P 500 recovered within days.

title: Trump wins the presidency
what: Donald Trump, a businessman who has never held office, won the US presidential election of 8 November against Hillary Clinton, carrying Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, while Clinton leads in the national vote. He promises tax cuts, less regulation, infrastructure spending and tariffs. After falling overnight, US shares rose to records, led by banks: the KBW bank index gained more than 17 percent in November.
why: Polls and markets expected the opposite; the 'Trump trade' lifted banks (Citigroup +15% in November) and the dollar, and his tariffs return as a theme in 2018 and above all in 2025.

title: The virus reaches Europe and Switzerland
what: The new coronavirus, which the World Health Organization declared an international emergency on 30 January, spread from China to northern Italy in late February, where towns were sealed off. Switzerland confirmed its first case on 25 February, a man in Ticino who had visited Milan, and on 28 February banned events with more than 1,000 people. Stock markets fell in the last week of the month.
why: The pandemic becomes a European event; the S&P 500's -8% in February is the first leg of the crash.

title: Pandemic: the world shuts down
what: The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March. Italy locked down on 9 March, the United States barred travellers from Europe, and on 16 March the Swiss government declared an 'extraordinary situation', closing schools, shops, restaurants and borders; on 20 March it announced a 42 billion franc aid package. Stock markets crashed: the Dow lost 7.8 percent on 9 March, 10 percent on 12 March and 12.9 percent on 16 March. The Fed cut rates to zero, and Congress passed a 2.2 trillion dollar relief law on 27 March.
why: The fastest crash in the game (S&P -13% in the month, Boeing -46%, Schlumberger -50%), a political and medical event; the bottom came on 23 March.

title: Locked-down world, rescued economies
what: Much of the world spent April at home. Governments and central banks kept adding to their rescue packages, and Switzerland's emergency loans and short-time work schemes are running. With new infections falling, Switzerland began to ease its restrictions step by step at the end of April.
why: The money from governments and the Fed, plus the first reopenings, drove a +13% month for the S&P 500, led by Amazon, Tesla and eBay, the winners of the lockdown.

title: Biden wins, and a vaccine works
what: Joe Biden won the US election of 3 November, with 306 electoral votes and about 51 percent of the vote, and was declared the winner by the media on 7 November; President Trump refuses to concede and claims fraud without evidence. On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech announced that their vaccine was about 90 percent effective in trials.
why: Two answers in one week: no contested-election chaos and a way out of the pandemic. The S&P 500 gained 11%, and the losers of the lockdown soared (Boeing +46%, Credit Suisse +33%).

title: A mob storms the Capitol
what: On 6 January, as Congress met to count the electoral votes, a crowd of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol after a rally at which the president repeated his false claims of a stolen election; five people died. Congress certified Biden's victory the next morning. The House impeached Trump for a second time on 13 January, and Joe Biden was sworn in on 20 January.
why: The low point of American democracy in the game's span; markets ignored it, but it shapes the politics of the 2024 election.

title: Bern breaks off the framework talks with the EU
what: On 26 May the Federal Council ended seven years of negotiations with the EU on an institutional framework agreement that was to bundle the bilateral treaties under common rules, saying differences over wage protection, state aid and the rights of EU citizens could not be bridged. Brussels regretted the decision and warned that existing agreements will not be updated.
why: Leaves Switzerland's EU relationship in limbo; Swiss researchers lose full access to EU programmes, and a new package is only agreed in 2024-25.

title: Russia invades Ukraine; Switzerland adopts the EU sanctions
what: On 24 February Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine from the north, east and south, with forces advancing on Kyiv; President Putin calls it a 'special military operation'. The West answered with sanctions, including cutting Russian banks off from the SWIFT payments system and freezing the central bank's reserves. On 28 February neutral Switzerland, after days of hesitation, adopted the EU sanctions in full and froze the assets of listed Russians, including Putin. Oil passed 100 dollars a barrel, and prices of metals, gas and grain jumped.
why: The largest war in Europe since 1945, and a turning point for Swiss neutrality. Commodity producers rose (Glencore +15% in the month) while the market fell; the energy shock feeds the inflation and rate rises of 2022.

title: Credit Suisse is forced into the arms of UBS
what: After bank failures in the United States, customers pulled billions of francs a day from Credit Suisse. On Sunday 19 March, under pressure from the Federal Council, the National Bank and the regulator FINMA, UBS agreed to take over its rival for 3 billion francs in UBS shares, 0.76 francs per Credit Suisse share against 1.86 on the Friday. The National Bank provides 100 billion francs of liquidity and the Confederation guarantees up to 9 billion francs of losses; the government used emergency law to bypass a shareholder vote.
why: The end of a 167-year-old Swiss bank and the third state rescue of a Swiss icon in the game; Credit Suisse shares fell 71% in the month. 'Too big to fail' has produced one even bigger bank.

title: Trump wins a second term
what: Donald Trump won the presidential election of 5 November against Vice President Kamala Harris, who replaced Joe Biden as candidate in July, with 312 electoral votes; Republicans also won the Senate. He promises tariffs, tax cuts and mass deportations. Tesla shares jumped on bets that its chief Elon Musk, who gave more than 130 million dollars to help Trump win, will benefit, and Tesla's market value passed one trillion dollars on 8 November.
why: Opens the tariff era of 2025; Tesla's +38% in November is the purest 'Trump trade' in the game, and it reversed in early 2025 when Musk's role in government hurt the brand.

title: Liberation Day: tariffs on the whole world
what: On 2 April President Trump announced tariffs on imports from almost every country: 10 percent for all from 5 April, and higher 'reciprocal' rates from 9 April, including 20 percent for the EU, 34 percent for China and 31 percent for Switzerland. Stock markets crashed for two days. On 9 April Trump paused the higher rates for 90 days, and the S&P 500 had its biggest one-day gain since 2008. The Swiss rate was met with incomprehension in Bern.
why: The largest US tariff rise in nearly a century; the market fell 10% in March on tariff fear and swung wildly in April, ending the month only 1% lower, as the pause turned into deals.

title: Trump hits Switzerland with a 39 percent tariff
what: On Swiss National Day, 1 August, Washington announced a 39 percent tariff on Swiss goods from 7 August, the highest in Europe and far above the 15 percent agreed with the EU, saying Switzerland refused to make significant concessions. Federal President Karin Keller-Sutter said the Federal Council was disappointed and that the rate was far higher than the one negotiated; the machinery industry fears for tens of thousands of jobs. Pharmaceuticals remain exempt for now.
why: Switzerland's biggest trade shock in decades, a national event; it lasted until a deal in November cut the rate to 15 percent in exchange for promised Swiss investment of 200 billion dollars in the United States.

title: Trump seizes Maduro and reaches for Greenland
what: On 3 January US airstrikes on Venezuela ended with the capture of President Nicolas Maduro and his wife; Switzerland froze his assets two days later. Trump's renewed threats to take Greenland from Denmark led Copenhagen to send troops to the island on 14 January with other European countries, and thousands protested in Copenhagen.
why: An America that uses force in its hemisphere and pressures its own allies; the Greenland dispute ended with a security agreement in September 2026. A month later the US and Israel went to war with Iran (Middle East arc).
